title: Lesson 2: Exploratory Data Analysis & Data Cleaning
text:
In our last session (Lesson 1), we read in and manipulated our data set, and merged in NDVI (greenness) data by census tract. In this session we continue to work with the data, doing some exploratory data analysis (EDA) and data cleaning. These are essential steps at the start of any new analysis.
Just as in Lesson 1, we first load any packages we need, then read in our data — using file.path() and the same data_raw / data_processed structure from your EOH635_project, not setwd().

title: Lesson 2: Exploratory Data Analysis & Data Cleaning
text:
Checking for Missing Values
Missing values can affect analysis, so it’s essential to check for them.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Questions to consider:

What variables have missing values?
How many missing values do you see for each?
Do you think this is a problem? Why or why not?







Note💡 Compare against the codebook — click to reveal





The Data Codebook lists the missingness that was deliberately built into this simulated dataset: mental_health (42), current_smoker (20), high_blood_pressure (12), stress (7), has_park (5), age (3), gender (2). If your colSums(is.na(data)) output matches that, your merge from Lesson 1 didn’t introduce (or lose) any missingness — which is exactly the kind of check worth doing after any merge.



For now we will not recode any of our missing variables. In some cases it makes sense to recode missing variables — particularly if we can infer their values from other variables in the data frame — but for now we’ll proceed without doing that. It’s good to be aware of which variables have missing values, since we’ll need to think about this later when conducting analyses.
Since you’ll be working with these data in your project analysis, be sure to take note of the variables that have missing values.

text:
Visual Exploration of Data
Let’s plot some key variables to understand their distributions and relationships.

Example 1: Histogram
Histograms are useful for visualizing the distribution of a single numeric variable. Let’s look at age.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Some of the values we see for age look suspicious — the ages > 110 are very suspect. Let’s recode those with age > 105 to be missing. (Another option would be to recode these to some high but plausible number, e.g. 100.)
There’s a trade-off here: we gain more missing values, or we introduce more uncertainty. This is a balancing act you’ll have to consider as you move forward with your own data analysis. Like most things, there isn’t necessarily one “right” answer — just be thoughtful, and document your choice.
Our new recoded age variable will be called r_age:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
We can check the number of missing values in the recoded and original age variables:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Note: after recoding, we have a few additional observations with missing age — that makes sense given the distribution we saw earlier.






Tip🧠 Your Turn



Recall from Lesson 1 that dplyr’s if_else() (typically used inside mutate()) is another way to do the same recoding ifelse() just did. Recreate r_age using mutate() and if_else() instead, calling the new column r_age2, and confirm it matches r_age (hint: a table of r_age == r_age2, or identical(), can confirm this — remember that NA == NA is NA, not TRUE, so a simple table() of the comparison is often clearer than identical() here).



Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






Note💡 Solution — click to reveal






Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
(Note: if_else() is stricter than base R’s ifelse() about types — it needs NA_real_ rather than a plain NA here, since age is a decimal/“double” column. This is a common if_else() gotcha worth remembering.)



Let’s recreate our histogram with the recoded age variable:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Our histogram no longer has the age outliers we observed earlier.


Example 2: Boxplot
Boxplots are helpful for identifying outliers and comparing distributions across categories.
Let’s look at the distribution of age by gender.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Question to consider: What is the relationship between gender identity and age?
Let’s look at high blood pressure, our primary outcome/dependent variable, by tree canopy cover (our primary exposure/independent variable):

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Note the as.character() wrapped around high_blood_pressure in the code above. Why do we need it? (Hint: try running the code without that wrapper. Hint 2: recall from the Data Codebook how high_blood_pressure is coded/stored.)






Note💡 Why as.character()? — click to reveal





high_blood_pressure is stored as an integer 0/1 flag, not a category. Without as.character(), ggplot treats it as a continuous numeric axis and tries to draw a single boxplot (or a strange, mostly-empty range of “groups” between 0 and 1) rather than two separate boxes for “0” and “1”. Wrapping it in as.character() (or factor()) tells ggplot to treat it as a categorical variable, so it draws one box per group as intended. This is the same integer-flags-that-are-really-categories issue you first ran into with str(data) back in Lesson 1.



Question to consider: Based on what you see here, what is the relationship between high blood pressure and % tree canopy cover?






Note



Remember this is a crude estimate of the relationship. We’ll use regression models later in the course to estimate this association, with modeling methods intended to help reduce bias in our estimate.

title: Data Codebook
text:
Area-Level (Tract-Level) Variables
These variables describe the census tract (geoid10) each participant lives in, rather than the participant individually — everyone living in the same tract shares the same value.

Population Density








Variable
Type
Description




popden_km
Numeric
Population density in the census tract (people per km²)





Traffic Volume
Variable: ctb1traff (Numeric — “Traffic density” per the official codebook)
Measured and estimated traffic volumes for major roads by road section are available annually from PennDOT (2005–present). Air pollution levels from traffic typically return to background levels within 100 to 300 m of roads. We calculated kernel densities of average daily traffic from PennDOT traffic data within 100 m and 300 m of road centerlines, on a 30 m grid, for southeastern Pennsylvania.

100 m was chosen based on work done for the New York City Community Air Survey.
300 m was chosen to account for the road width of wider roads.

The variable in the data set represents the average of the 100 m kernel-density average daily traffic in the participant’s residential census tract. Higher value = greater traffic volume.
Data sources

Background: Annual Average Daily Traffic by road segment, from the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation (PennDOT), Bureau of Planning and Research, Geographic Information Division.
Data obtained: Downloaded from www.pasda.psu.edu (2005–2015 downloaded 11/4/2016; 2016–2017 downloaded 4/26/2017).



Land Cover: Tree Canopy & Grass/Shrub Cover








Variable
Type
Description




hrlctree
Numeric
Tree canopy cover (proportion in the census tract)


hrlcgrass_shrub
Numeric
Grass or shrub cover (proportion in the census tract)



Derived from the Philadelphia Land Cover Raster, which provides data on surface types in Philadelphia in 2008 and an update in 2018 (the 2015 value in this data set was created using linear interpolation between the two). The data identifies seven categories: tree canopy, grass/shrub, bare earth, water, buildings, roads, and other paved surfaces. When tree canopy covers another surface type, that area is placed in the tree canopy category. Data were gathered with the assistance of the University of Vermont Spatial Analysis Laboratory.
You can calculate a total vegetation measure by summing hrlctree and hrlcgrass_shrub together.


Tract-Level Sociodemographic Composition








Variable
Type
Description




race_blackNH
Numeric
Proportion non-Hispanic Black residents in the census tract


race_whiteNH
Numeric
Proportion non-Hispanic White residents in the census tract


race_hisp
Numeric
Proportion Hispanic residents in the census tract


Educ_ltHS
Numeric
Proportion of tract residents with less than a high school education


Educ_ltba
Numeric
Proportion of tract residents with less than a bachelor’s degree


pov_allage
Numeric
Proportion of tract residents living in poverty


unemployed
Numeric
Proportion of tract unemployed



Data sources

Background: The American Community Survey (ACS), administered by the U.S. Census Bureau, is a nationwide survey providing social, economic, housing, and demographic data. The Census Bureau combines five consecutive years to produce estimates at the census tract level.
Data obtained: ACS 5-year average data for 2017–2021, downloaded from the U.S. Census Bureau. Race/ethnicity variables were calculated as the percentage of persons in the census tract identifying with each category, across all age/gender groups. Data may be missing if a measure was suppressed by the Census Bureau due to low sample size (to protect against potentially identifying information).



Crime Variables








Variable
Type
Description




ctviolra
Numeric
Violent crime rate — units unconfirmed, see flag below


ctviolkm
Numeric
Violent crime rate per km² in the census tract



Police-reported crime data is available from OpenDataPhilly. Yearly crime rates and densities (per square mile/km) for the City of Philadelphia were created for calendar years 2006–2016. Crimes are categorized, with rates/densities available for violent crime, narcotic drug violations, and property crime, summarized by 2010 U.S. Census Tract. These rates were generated to provide objective measures of neighborhood safety, and can be used to explore the influence of crime and safety on health outcomes and behaviors.






Warning⚠️ Unresolved: units for ctviolra



Two source documents disagree on the unit for ctviolra, and this hasn’t been confirmed yet:

Classdata_arealevelmeasures_description.docx describes it as a rate per 10,000 population.
The official codebook.xlsx (and the create_data.R script that generated it) describes it as “Total violent crime incidents per 1,000 residents.”

Leaving this unresolved for now, per instructor note — don’t state a specific unit for ctviolra in student-facing material until this is confirmed.








Note



The source .docx also lists a missing-data sentinel value of 9999999999 for the crime variables. That value does not actually appear anywhere in class_data_raw.csv (checked directly) — it looks like a leftover description from the original real-data source system, not something present in this simulated class dataset. No special recoding is needed for ctviolra/ctviolkm on that account.

section: Creating a numeric version of the education variable
text:
Creating a numeric version of the education variable
Sometimes it’s helpful to convert a character variable into a numeric variable — this can be very helpful when conducting quantitative analysis. Let’s do this now, using base R’s ifelse():

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
What happened here? This line creates a new variable called num_education, a numeric version of education, using ifelse():

The code checks each value of education.
If the value is "< Bachelor's" (less than a bachelor’s degree), num_education is set to 0.
For all other values (presumably at least a bachelor’s degree), num_education is set to 1.

So this line recodes a categorical education variable into a binary (0/1) numeric variable, where:

0 = less than a bachelor’s degree
1 = bachelor’s degree or higher

Note: in R there are lots of ways to do the same thing. Another way to recode this variable is with the dplyr package (loaded as part of tidyverse) instead of base R’s ifelse().






Tip🧠 Your Turn



dplyr’s equivalent of ifelse() is if_else(), typically used inside mutate(). Try rewriting the num_education recode above using data %>% mutate(...) and if_else() instead of base R. Call the new column num_education2 so you can compare it to the original.

title: Lesson 1: Intro to R and Handling Data
text:
Load another dataset
You’ll find an additional data frame, which contains neighborhood-level (tract-level) data on NDVI (greenness), called PHL_NDVI_summer_annual.csv. (For the other tract-level environmental and sociodemographic variables already in data — like hrlctree or pov_allage — see the Data Codebook.)
This data frame shows the median value of the summertime NDVI value for each census tract in Philadelphia — that is, how green each census tract is. NDVI stands for Normalized Difference Vegetation Index. NDVI ranges in value from -1 to 1.

Negative values represent water.
Values close to 1 mean dense vegetation.
Values close to 0 mean a lack of vegetation (there might instead be lots of concrete).

This page tells us a bit more about NDVI.
Let’s read in that data (again, in the browser we first fetch it from the web; in RStudio you’d just need it in your working directory):

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

But we want to know how green the neighborhoods of our study participants are.
To do so, we’re going to link the NDVI data frame to our primary data frame using a common variable found in both.

The common variable is called geoid10. In our class data frame, geoid10 refers to the census tract in which the study participant lives. In the NDVI data frame, GEOID10 refers to each unique Philadelphia census tract.
In order for the merge/linkage to work, both variables have to be in the same format (both character, or both numeric, etc.). Let’s check on this now.
